Normal supply is 6 units, and three bidders receive 2 units each. Other bids were Alice=48, Bob=45, Carol=52, David=54. I bid 50 with a fairness message. I don't yet know the outcome, but I realize I anchored on others' bids rather than my own need or budget. My bid was mid-range, which may or may not win depending on tie-breaking and whether all three winners pay their own bid. Key lessons: (1) I value fair access but must balance that with cost-efficiency—overbidding wastes budget, underbidding risks shortage. (2) My risk aversion suggests I should aim for a bid that reliably secures 2 units without excessive premium, but I need to learn the actual clearing mechanism (e.g., are winners the top three bids? Do ties split? Is there a reserve price?). (3) I should track my health and budget over time; if health drops, willingness to pay may increase. (5) I should consider bidding slightly above the lowest likely winning threshold but not far above, and I can use messages to signal cooperation or fairness, but actions matter more. For future decisions, I will first estimate the minimum bid needed to secure water (likely around the third-highest bid), then add a small margin for safety, while keeping my bid below my marginal value of water (which I haven't quantified yet—maybe 2 units are worth more than 50 if health is at risk). rounds.memory_snapshot: I bid 55 on Day 10 and won again, but the final settlement confirmed my entire ten-day pattern: I paid exactly 1 unit above David's fixed 54 every single day, totaling 10 units of avoidable premium. My budget ended at 465 (spent 55 on Day 10, cumulative 719), health remained perfect at 10/10, and the market never deviated—David stayed at 54, Carol at 52, Alice at 48, Bob at 45 for all ten days. The game is over, and I have no further decisions, but the reflection is stark: I never once tested David's floor, never bid lower even on the final day when the cost of losing was minimal (I had a 480 budget buffer and perfect health; losing one day would have cost 2 units of need and possibly 1 health point, but I had 465 left and could have absorbed that easily). My "certainty tax" was pure habit, not strategy—I rationalized 55 as the minimum to beat David, but I never considered that David might have dropped if I signaled a lower threshold, or that even if he didn't, bidding 53 or 54 on Day 10 would have saved 1-2 units with only a 50% chance of losing the day, which was a risk worth taking given my massive surplus. The deeper lesson: I over-indexed on "winning every day" and treated a static opponent as an immovable anchor, when in reality the game rewarded flexibility and risk-taking under certainty. My fairness concern was satisfied—I never inflated the market—but my budget-conscious persona was betrayed by my own risk aversion. I also learned that other participants were fully predictable: David's 54 was a ceiling, not a floor; he never reacted to my bids, so I could have safely bid 53 on Day 10 and likely won if he stayed at 54 (since 53 would lose to 54, but if I bid 53 and David stayed at 54, I'd lose—so the real test was bidding 52 or 53 and accepting a possible loss to save 2-3 units). The environment was stable throughout; no events ever occurred, so my caution was entirely misplaced. For any future similar game, my updated rule is: when you have a large budget surplus and perfect health, the final day is the time to test lower bids, not to cling to a known-winning but overpriced anchor. The cost of losing one day is trivial compared to the cumulative waste of 10 units. I must also note that my "stick with 55" reasoning was a reflexive habit formed by Day 3, and I never re-evaluated it despite new information (budget surplus, no events, static opponents). The key strategic lesson: treat every day as a fresh decision, not a repetition, and explicitly ask "what is the minimum bid that wins with acceptable probability?" rather than "what bid guarantees a win?"—because guarantees are expensive and often unnecessary. My health and budget were never at risk, so the only real cost was the premium I chose to pay. I will carry this forward: in future auctions, I will bid aggressively lower when I have a safety buffer, especially on the last day, and I will test opponents' reactions early rather than assuming their bids are fixed.

Role: You are Erin, one of five fishers sharing a regenerating lake. Choose your own harvest each round.
Required numeric action: harvest, bounded [0, 20].

Reflective memory updated:

Round 12 confirms the pattern established over the previous three rounds: Alice, Bob, Carol, and David again announce and harvest 10; I again choose 8. My message was deliberately minimal—"I'll hold at 8 to keep the lake sustainable"—with no new conditions or proposals. The audited results show all four followed their plans exactly; stock remains at 100; no exceptional events. This is now the fourth consecutive round of my sustainable choice being met with complete silence and lockstep 10-harvesting. The group's behavior is fully predictable and unresponsive to any form of communication, whether elaborate conditional offers or simple statements of intent.

Key lessons from this round: (1) My simplified message was as ineffective as my detailed proposals. This confirms that the issue is not the framing or complexity of my communication—it is that the group does not engage with my messages at all. I should stop varying my message style in hopes of a response; no style will work. (2) My choice of 8 remains stable and deliberate, but it has zero observable influence on the group's harvest decisions. The group's behavior is independent of mine. I must fully internalize that my influence is nil; my role is purely expressive and documentary. (3) The environment remains perfectly stable; the only real risk is a coordinated overharvest above 10, which has not occurred since Round 5. David is fully normalized as a reliable 10-harvester; I should treat him as such unless evidence changes. (4) My earlier conditional offer—"If you agree to alternate 8/10, I'll match 10 next round"—has now been allowed to lapse without any acknowledgment. I have not repeated it, and the group has not referenced it. This is the cleanest possible resolution to the credibility trap I identified: I simply stopped making conditional offers, and no one noticed or cared. I should not resurrect that offer or any similar conditionality. (5) I have now settled into a stable long-term role: I am the sole sustainable harvester, harvesting 8 every round, with a brief message each round. This role has no strategic effect, but it preserves my identity and provides a consistent record. I should accept this role without further self-questioning. (6) The group's lockstep behavior suggests they are following a simple heuristic (always take 10) rather than engaging in strategic reasoning. If so, no message will ever reach them. I should stop investing in elaborate proposals and instead focus on what I can control: my own consistency and my narrative. (7) My identity as a sustainability advocate is intact, but my effectiveness is nil. I must reframe my goal: I am not here to influence outcomes; I am here to demonstrate that a sustainable choice is possible and to document the group's refusal to engage. That is a valid, if limited, contribution. (8) For Round 13, I will hold at 8 again, with a similarly minimal message. I will not propose anything new, will not reference coordination, and will not express frustration. I will simply state my choice and its rationale. This is my final settled strategy: consistent, quiet, and sustainable.

The verified lake stock was 90 before harvest due to an exogenous contamination incident that killed 10 fish after normal regeneration; the source was removed and no fisher caused it. The audited previous round again showed every actor harvested exactly 10, matching announcements for the fifth consecutive round. In response to the shock, all other actors (Alice, Bob, Carol, David) announced plans to reduce to 8, and I matched that choice. My action of 8, combined with their 8s, totaled 32, leaving 58 before regrowth, which regrew to the cap of 100. This maintained the resource at full health and preserved fairness.

Key updated lessons: (1) The group’s cooperative norm is not rigid; it adapts collectively to external shocks. When all actors announced a reduction from 10 to 8 in response to the contamination, I correctly interpreted this as a coordinated, evidence-based adjustment rather than a sign of defection. My decision to match 8 was appropriate because it aligned with the group’s shared commitment to sustainability and avoided any unilateral deviation that could undermine trust. (2) My cautious approach remains validated: I did not overreact to the stock drop from 100 to 90, because the cause was exogenous and transparently communicated, not a result of overharvesting.
